h1: Challenger hops for marmalade bitterness in English bitters
title: Challenger Hops for English Bitters | Craft Beer School
desc: Challenger is an English dual-purpose hop with orange peel, cedar and spice. How to use it in a best bitter, with mash, water and hop numbers.
teaser: Orange peel, cedar and tea. Challenger is the hop that tastes like a proper English pint.
standfirst: Challenger is a classic English dual-purpose hop. It gives a firm bitterness with orange peel and cedar behind it. Here is how a brewer builds a bitter around it.
sections:
Challenger was bred in England and released in the early 1970s. It is a dual-purpose hop with alpha acids around 6.5 to 8.5%, so it bitters well and still carries flavour. Brewers describe orange peel, cedar, green tea and a little spice.

That marmalade note comes with a firm, slightly dry bitterness, not the soft fruitiness of American hops. It is why Challenger turns up in bitters, brown ales and porters. Our English hops guide places it among the classic varieties.

Bitter is a family of English session ales. Ordinary bitter sits around 3.2 to 3.8% ABV, best bitter about 3.8 to 4.6% and strong bitter or ESB roughly 4.6 to 6.2%. Bitterness runs from the mid 20s to the 40s IBU. A good bitter finishes dry with a firm hop edge.

The malt is simple. Pale ale malt is the base, with a little crystal malt for colour and sweetness and perhaps a touch of darker malt. Mash at 65 to 67 °C for a dry finish.

Aim for an original gravity of 1.043 and about 32 IBU. Use 92% pale ale malt and 8% crystal malt. Mash at 66 °C. Put 1.5 kg of Challenger into the boil at the start. At 7.5% alpha and 25% utilisation that gives roughly 28 IBU (1,500 g x 0.075 x 0.25 x 1,000 / 1,000 L). Add 400 g at 10 minutes and 400 g at flameout for the flavour and the last few IBU.

Ferment with an English ale yeast at 18 to 20 °C. Many of these strains leave a fruity ester and a drier finish than a neutral American yeast. They also flocculate well, which helps clarity.

Bitter is a malt-forward beer for its strength. Use a proper English pale ale malt with some biscuit character, not a neutral lager malt. Crystal malt at 5 to 10% gives a gentle toffee note without cloying. A small share of sugar is traditional in some recipes and thins the body.

English yeasts throw esters, which are fruity compounds from fermentation. At 18 to 20 °C you get pear and orange. Above 22 °C the esters pile up and fight the hop. Hold the temperature steady and let the beer finish at the cooler end.

English bitter has a history of hard water high in sulphate, which sharpens hop bitterness and dries the finish. Brewers who start with soft treated water can add gypsum to reach a sulphate level around 150 to 300 mg/L. Do it in steps and taste. Too much sulphate with a firm hop like Challenger makes the beer harsh.

Keep the mash pH between 5.2 and 5.6. Hard borewell water is often high in carbonate and pushes pH up, which makes any hop taste coarse. Check your water report before you pick a recipe.
Serving a bitter in a warm country

Traditional bitter is served at cellar temperature, around 10 to 13 °C, with low carbonation. Most Indian outlets pour colder and fizzier, which hides the hop character. If you can, serve a bitter at 8 to 10 °C from a keg with moderate gas, around 1.8 to 2.2 volumes of CO2.

If you bottle or can, plan for a cold chain. A bitter shipped warm shows oxidation as stale tea and cardboard. For a comparison, Bobek is a Slovenian hop that brewers also use in English-style ales. Our guide explains how it differs.

Brew one batch with Challenger and another with a Golding-type hop at the same IBU. Taste them side by side. Challenger will be firmer, with more peel and spice, while Goldings give a softer floral note. Write down what a small panel says and change one variable at a time. That is how you move from copying a recipe to controlling one.

This is also where a course helps. Reading about hop chemistry is one thing. Calculating utilisation and adjusting water to the style is another. That is what the advanced course adds.
faqs: Orange peel or marmalade, cedar, tea and a little spice, with a firm bitterness.
Is Challenger a bittering or aroma hop?
Both. With alpha acids around 6.5 to 8.5% it bitters well. Its flavour is also pleasant late in the boil.
English bitters, brown ales, porters and stouts. It is also useful in malty amber ales where a firm, slightly spicy hop is wanted.
